content: Endometritis refers to the inflammation or irritation of the inner lining of the uterus, known as the endometrium. Symptoms of Endometritis: Patients may experience abdominal distension or swelling. Abnormal vaginal bleeding is a common symptom. There may be abnormal vaginal discharge. Discomfort during bowel movements can occur, and constipation may be present. Fever ranging from 100 to 104 degrees Fahrenheit is often observed. General discomfort, uneasiness, or a feeling of being unwell (malaise) is frequently reported. Lower abdominal or pelvic pain, often described as uterine pain, is a hallmark symptom. Causes of Endometritis: The condition is typically caused by infections, including those from organisms such as Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, tuberculosis, or a combination of normal vaginal bacteria. It is more likely to develop following a miscarriage or childbirth, particularly after prolonged labor or a cesarean section. Medical procedures that involve entering the uterus through the cervix, such as dilation and curettage (D&C), hysteroscopy, or the placement of an intrauterine device (IUD), increase the risk of endometritis. Endometritis can also occur concurrently with other pelvic infections, such as acute salpingitis, acute cervicitis, or sexually transmitted diseases (STDs). When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: You should schedule an appointment with your healthcare provider if you experience symptoms of endometritis. Immediate medical attention is necessary if symptoms occur after recent childbirth, miscarriage, abortion, IUD placement, or any uterine surgery. Diagnosis: A healthcare provider will perform a physical examination and a pelvic exam. Tenderness in the lower abdomen may be noted, and bowel sounds may be reduced. The uterus and cervix may be tender during the pelvic exam, and cervical discharge may be present. Diagnostic tests may include: Cervical cultures to test for Chlamydia, Gonorrhea, and other organisms. Endometrial biopsy. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) to assess inflammation. Laparoscopy for direct visualization. White blood cell (WBC) count to detect infection. Microscopic examination of any discharge (wet prep). Treatment Options: Antibiotics are the primary treatment to address the infection and prevent complications. It is crucial to complete the full course of antibiotics as prescribed, especially if they are given following a gynecological procedure. Hospitalization may be required for complicated cases, such as those with severe symptoms or postpartum infections. Additional treatments may include: Intravenous (IV) fluids. Rest. Treatment of sexual partners if the condition is caused by a sexually transmitted infection. Where to Find Medical Care: Seek care at hospitals or clinics equipped to treat endometritis. Prognosis: Most cases of endometritis resolve with appropriate antibiotic treatment. If left untreated, the condition can lead to severe infections and complications affecting pelvic organs, reproductive health, and overall well-being. Possible Complications: Infertility. Pelvic peritonitis, which is a generalized pelvic infection. Formation of pelvic or uterine abscesses. Septicemia (blood infection). Septic shock, a life-threatening condition. Prevention: Endometritis caused by sexually transmitted infections can be prevented by: Early diagnosis and complete treatment of STDs in both the patient and their sexual partners. Practicing safe sex, such as using condoms. The risk of endometritis is reduced when healthcare providers use sterile techniques during childbirth, abortion, IUD placement, or other gynecological procedures.
